extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators / patent counsel evaluating or briefing Section 101 (Alice) motions
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating motions to dismiss, motions for judgment on the pleadings, or summary judgment under 35 U.S.C. § 101 (the Alice framework) — i.e., whether claimed subject matter is directed to an abstract idea and whether the claims supply an inventive concept, and whether that question can be resolved pre- or post-claim-construction or discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed to an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the representative claim is 'directed to an abstract idea' (e.g., organizing data, time stamping, using keywords to search hierarchical data, fundamental economic practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine whether the claim as a whole is aimed at an abstract idea (examples in the cases include data organization, time stamping, recommending products based on location). If a claim is found 'directed to an abstract idea,' the inquiry proceeds to whether there is an inventive concept. The record (pleadings, specification, prosecution history) can inform whether the claim is a particular technological improvement or merely an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept / whether claim elements supply something 'more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the challenged claim elements, 'individually and as an ordered combination, lack an inventive concept' and thus fail to transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look for an 'inventive concept' beyond the abstract idea — e.g., unconventional technological solutions, novel combinations or specific improvements to technology. Whether an inventive concept exists is often factbound; parties should present evidence (specification, prior art, expert testimony) because courts frequently find genuine disputes of material fact on this point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claimed computer functions are 'well-understood, routine, conventional activities' previously known to the industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendants bear responsibility to provide evidence that elements are conventional; lacking such evidence, courts often deny eligibility motions. Determinations of conventionality are frequently questions of fact for which discovery and expert input may be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for claim construction before §101 determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether claim construction (Markman) is necessary before resolving a §101 question because disputed claim term meanings may affect whether a claim is abstract or contains an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many courts defer ruling on eligibility until after claim construction if key terms are in dispute or if the proper scope of preemption or inventive-concept analysis depends on a 'settled interpretation of the claim language.' If claim construction will materially affect the eligibility analysis, dismissal is often denied as premature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prematurity at pleading stage / need for factual development
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether ruling on eligibility at the Rule 12(b)(6)/12(c) pleading stage or early summary judgment is premature due to lack of factual record, discovery, or expert evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts frequently deny or deny without prejudice motions to dismiss on §101 grounds where there has been no discovery, no expert evidence, or where factual disputes (e.g., about conventionality) remain. Defendants seeking early resolution should show there is no set of facts that could make the claims eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative claim selection and adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: When using a representative claim for a §101 motion, evaluate (1) whether the non-representative claims are adequately represented by the chosen representative claim, (2) whether claim construction issues must be decided first, and (3) whether there are any set of facts that could prove eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts scrutinize attempts to decide eligibility based on a single representative claim; if defendants fail to articulate why dependent or other claims are captured by the representative claim or do not show they relate to the same abstract idea, courts often deny the motion. Parties should justify representativeness or address each asserted claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether parties dispute key terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify whether the parties 'dispute the meaning of various terms among various claims' — such disputes can preclude resolving §101 early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the parties disagree on claim meanings that bear on the Alice test (e.g., scope of 'data', 'transformative concept'), courts usually find claim construction necessary and defer eligibility rulings until the terms are construed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of physical structures / hardware limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the claims recite physical structures (e.g., 'discount vehicle with information', specialized sensors, multiple hardware components) or are 'limited to the field' of a technology in a way that makes them non-abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that include concrete physical structures, particular hardware configurations, or limitations tied to a technological field or problem are less likely to be deemed abstract. Courts have relied on such hardware recitations and field-specific limits to find claims directed to technological improvements rather than abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification/prosecution history showing technological improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the specification or prosecution history 'articulates a solution to problems' in a technological realm or states novelty of a particular organization/approach, supporting an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may rely on statements in the specification and prosecution history to infer that claims embody a particular technological improvement (e.g., hierarchical organization, specialized databases, sensor techniques). Such support can create factual issues precluding dismissal and bolster a finding of inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear and convincing evidence / burden at early stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the movant has met the applicable proof standard (e.g., the defendant must meet a 'clear and convincing evidence' standard for certain invalidity contentions) when seeking dismissal on eligibility grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At early stages, courts have denied motions where defendants failed to meet the requisite burden of proof (for instance, failing to present clear and convincing evidence). Parties should be prepared to meet the appropriate evidentiary standard for invalidity-type assertions at the procedural posture of the motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption / scope-of-preemption considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the claim preempts a fundamental principle or would monopolize an abstract idea, and whether claim construction is needed to determine the scope of preemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preemption concerns factor into the §101 inquiry. Courts have stated that claim construction aids in determining the scope of preemption, and if preemption cannot be assessed without construing terms, the eligibility decision is deferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to identify a representative claim defeats early motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the movant has 'identified a representative claim' when asking the court to resolve eligibility across multiple asserted claims; failure to do so can be a basis to deny the motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some courts have denied eligibility motions where neither party identified a representative claim or where the movant focused almost exclusively on one independent claim while moving against several dependent claims. Properly articulated representation or per-claim analysis is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of a possible set of facts making claims eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether there 'are any set of facts that could be proven that would result in a determination that one or more of the claims are eligible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the complaint or record plausibly alleges facts that, if proven, would show eligibility (e.g., novel technical details, unconventional combination), courts often deny dismissal without prejudice, allowing factual development.

rubrics_metrics.name: When courts grant dismissal vs. deny: examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize patterns where courts have granted dismissal (e.g., claims purely time-stamping with no inventive concept) versus where courts deny or defer (e.g., disputes over conventionality, need for claim construction, presence of hardware/technical improvements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use case examples to predict outcomes: courts granted dismissal where claims plainly recited an abstract idea with no added inventive concept; courts denied or deferred where specification suggested technological improvements, physical structures were recited, or factual disputes over conventionality/inventive concept existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of multiple defendants / impact across related cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor in whether a §101 ruling would 'affect all defendants in all pending cases' or whether all defendants have had an opportunity to participate; courts may defer resolution to allow full participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple related cases or defendants are involved, courts sometimes decline to address Alice issues before consolidating input from all parties or where not all defendants have raised §101; procedural fairness and the practical effect of a ruling on many parties can lead to postponement.
